title_eng: From radial to aortic pressure: In silico data-driven estimation using an autoencoder
title_kor: From radial to aortic pressure: In silico data-driven estimation using an autoencoder
abstract:
From radial to aortic pressure: In silico data-driven estimation using 
an autoencoder
Hangsik Shin *
Department of Medical Informatics and Statistics, Asan Medical Center, Brain Korea 21 Project, University of Ulsan College of Medicine, Seoul 05505, Republic of Korea
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Aortic blood pressure
Autoencoder
Radial blood pressure
Transfer function
Machine learning
ABSTRACT
Accurately estimating aortic blood pressure (ABP) waveforms is crucial for cardiovascular health assessment and 
clinical intervention. However, direct measurement of ABP is challenging owing to its invasiveness and the 
complex arterial dynamics involved. To address this issue, we introduce a machine learning-based approach 
utilizing a cross-encoder with an autoencoder–hetero-decoder (AE–HD) architecture. This transfer function is 
designed to precisely convert radial blood pressure (RBP) waveforms into ABP waveforms. The training phase 
comprises an auto-encoding step to learn latent RBP representations and a hetero-decoding step to estimate the 
ABP waveform from the encoded RBP waveform. The proposed model was trained and evaluated on in silico 
datasets, achieving mean absolute errors of 0.53 ± 0.37, 0.46 ± 0.49, and 0.30 ± 0.28 mmHg for the total 
waveform, systolic blood pressure, and diastolic blood pressure, respectively, and 2.14 ± 2.25 % for the 
augmentation index estimation. Although the AE–HD model demonstrated high accuracy in these simulations, its 
generalizability to real-world clinical settings remains to be established. Further validation using real patient 
data and diverse clinical scenarios is planned. This research holds potential for improving non-invasive car-
diovascular monitoring and enhancing patient care across clinical contexts.

1. Introduction
Precise estimation of aortic blood pressure (ABP) waveforms is 
indispensable for cardiovascular risk stratification and evidence-based 
clinical decision-making. However, direct ABP measurement remains 
clinically impractical owing to its invasive nature and the intricate he-
modynamic interplay within the arterial system. To address this issue, a 
method that involves capturing the radial blood pressure (RBP) wave-
form and then converting it using a generalized transfer function (GTF) 
has gained prominence [1,2]. The GTF-based approach uses non- 
invasive techniques to measure peripheral artery pressures, such as 
radial or brachial pressures, and employs mathematical models or al-
gorithms to derive estimates of the central ABP waveform.
The RBP and ABP waveforms have intricate differences owing to the 
complex interactions within the arterial system. Although both wave-
forms share certain characteristics, including the basic shape of the 
pressure curve, they differ in aspects such as the wave reflections, 
arterial compliance, and influence of arterial stiffness. Understanding 
these disparities is crucial for accurate cardiovascular assessment. Once 
defined, GTFs can be used to accurately estimate central BP using 
peripheral BP measurements. However, GTF-based ABP estimation may 
not be suitable for handling inter- and intra-subject variability because it 
assumes a constant relationship for all individuals and their cardiovas-
cular status [3,4].
Neural networks offer powerful advantages in nonlinear modeling, 
particularly in complex and intricate systems. Their unique ability to 
capture complex relationships within a dataset allows them to accu-
rately represent complex nonlinearities that traditional linear models 
struggle to capture. With their layered architecture and tunable pa-
rameters, neural networks can identify complex patterns, adapt to 
changing contexts, and learn from diverse datasets. Owing to these 
characteristics, machine-learning models based on neural networks are 
used for RBP-to-ABP waveform conversion. Magbool et al. showed that a 
hybrid model based on multi-layer perceptrons was effective for ABP 
waveform estimation [5]. Xaio et al. used a convolutional neural net-
work–bidirectional long short-term memory model for RBP-to-ABP 
waveform conversion; they obtained root mean square errors (RMSEs) 
of 2.95 ± 0.16, 3.34 ± 0.91, and 2.41 ± 0.18 mmHg for total waveform, 
arterial systolic blood pressure (SBP), and arterial diastolic blood pres-
sure (DBP) estimation, respectively [6]. Recently, Liu et al. reported that

An autoencoder (AE) has a manifold neural network architecture, 
comprising an encoder for the transformation of input data into a lower- 
dimensional latent space representation and a subsequent decoder for 
estimating the original input data using this latent space representation 
[8]. Despite its apparent simplicity, the AE demonstrates extensive 
utility across a range of applications, including feature extraction, 
dimensionality reduction, noise mitigation, anomaly identification, and 
transfer learning. Notably, the manifold learning capacity to ameliorate 
errors attributable to stochastic factors, exemplified by input data 
variability, is well-established. This capacity stems from its emphasis on 
dimensionality reduction while retaining the inherent data structure 
[9]. AEs are capable of extracting key features while mitigating the ef-
fects of differences arising from high variability or randomness of the 
input data [10].
The aim of this study was to develop and implement a deep learning 
model based on an AE structure for effectively estimating the ABP 
waveform from an RBP waveform. Given the intricate nature of the 
cardiovascular system and nonlinear relationships present in physio-
logical data, our primary goal was to leverage the AE’s capabilities in 
capturing complex patterns and representations. Through this innova-
tive approach, we aimed to enhance the accuracy and reliability of ABP 
waveform estimation, thereby contributing to improved non-invasive 
cardiovascular monitoring techniques and ultimately advancing pa-
tient care in clinical settings. To achieve this, we utilized in silico 
datasets to rigorously test and validate the model’s performance under 
controlled, idealized conditions. This controlled testing environment 
allowed us to assess the model’s core capabilities without the variability 
introduced by real-world data, which may include noise, measurement 
errors, and other complexities that could obscure the model’s true per-
formance. Such an approach ensures the model’s robustness and reli-
ability, which are crucial for subsequent applications using real patient 
data.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Dataset: Simulated pulse wave dataset
This study used a publicly available dataset of simulated pulse wave 
signals from 4,374 healthy virtual subjects aged between 25 and 75 
years [11]. The simulated in silico pulse wave dataset was a computer- 
generated dataset created through computational modeling of the car-
diovascular characteristics of healthy adults obtained from a literature 
review. Table 1 displays the number of subjects grouped by age and BP 
range. This dataset includes pulse wave information collected from 
commonly used photoplethysmography measurement sites (arteries), 
such as finger, radial, brachial, and aortic arteries. A comparison of the 
hemodynamic parameters or pulse wave morphology with findings from 
in vivo studies showed substantial agreement [7,12,13]. Among the 
arterial waveforms at various locations included in the simulated pulse 
wave dataset, we used the radial artery and ABP waveforms. The dataset 
had a sampling frequency of 500 Hz and contained one representative 
pulse waveform per measurement location. Each of these pulse wave-
forms had a different beat interval and therefore a different number of 
samples; therefore, we adjusted the number of samples in all the pulse 
waveforms to 512, using spline interpolation to equalize the length of 
the sequence input to the training model.
2.2. Convolutional Cross-Encoder
A cross-encoder has some commonality with an AE in that it encodes 
the input data and then decodes it using a layer that has a symmetrical 
structure with respect to the layer used for encoding. However, unlike an 
AE, which estimates the input data as it is, a cross-encoder estimates 
data different from the input data. In a network with this enco-
der–decoder structure, the encoder is an artificial neural network that 
can learn a compressed representation of the input data, called a latent 
representation or coding, without any supervision and act as a feature 
extractor. The decoder is a generator that estimates the waveform from 
the latent representation. The cross-encoder used in this study consists of 
a combination of an encoder and a decoder, namely, an AE and a hetero- 
decoder (HD). As shown in Fig. 1, its input has the structure of an RBP 
waveform, whereas the output has the structure of an ABP waveform. 
Both the AE and HD are composed of six convolutional layers each. Here, 
the AE is responsible for learning the latent representation of the RBP 
waveform and reconstructing it as a hidden feature (auto-encoding), and 
the HD is responsible for reconstructing the ABP waveform from the 
latent representation of the RBP waveform (hetero-decoding).
The layer-by-layer information of the AE–HD used in this study is 
presented in Table 2. The convolutional layer of the AE was designed in 
such a way that as the layer deepened, the number of filters increased 
and the kernel size decreased; the HD was designed as a symmetrical 
structure with a deconvolutional layer. The stride of all the convolu-
tional and deconvolutional layers was set to two, and a rectified linear 
unit (ReLU) [14] was used as the activation function. The process of 
developing and verifying the cross-encoder is shown in Fig. 2. In the 
auto-encoding stage, the model was trained with RBP as both input and 
output, whereas the latent representation of the RBP waveform was 
learned in the latent layer. In the next step, that is, hetero-decoding, the 
encoder part (EA) trained in the auto-encoding step was used; however, 
the weights were no longer updated, and only the decoder part (HD) was 
trained. In this case, the input was the RBP waveform, the output was the 
ABP waveform, and the HD was trained to estimate the ABP waveform 
from the latent representation of the RBP converted through the encoder 
(EA) of the AE. The training was performed with the training set, and 
then the test was performed using the test set with the trained model 
independent of the training set.
